periodic-phenomena-s1.title: A periodic function $f$
periodic-phenomena-s1.text: The graph shows a periodic function $f$ on $[0, 12]$. On each piece, $f$ is linear.

plot.label: Graph of a periodic function f made of straight pieces: it rises from (0, 2) to (1, 5), falls to (3, -1), rises through (4, 2) to (5, 5), falls to (7, -1), rises to (9, 5), falls to (11, -1) and rises to (12, 2)

periodic-phenomena-s2.title: Power use of an office building

table.caption: Power use $P(t)$ of an office building, in kilowatts, $t$ hours after midnight on a weekday. The pattern repeats every 24 hours.

why.correct: The highest points are at $x = 1$, $5$ and $9$, four units apart, and the whole pattern on $[1, 5]$ repeats on $[5, 9]$. The period is $4$.
options: From one highest point to the next is $5 - 1 = 4$, and the graph matches from there on.
That is the distance from a highest point ($x = 1$) to the next lowest point ($x = 3$), only part of a cycle.
Shifting by 6 does not keep the outputs: $f(1) = 5$ but $f(7) = -1$.
$f(x + 12) = f(x)$ does hold, but 12 is three periods. The period is the smallest positive value that works.

items.q: The pattern in the graph continues for all $x$. What is $f(39)$?

mistakes.why: That is $f(40) = f(0)$. Subtract whole periods from 39: $39 - 9 \cdot 4 = 3$, so $f(39) = f(3)$.
That is $f(1)$. $39 = 9 \cdot 4 + 3$, so the input lands at $3$ in the first cycle, not at $1$.

why.correct: The period is $4$ and $39 = 9 \cdot 4 + 3$, so $f(39) = f(3) = -1$.

items.q: What is the average rate of change of $f$ on $[5, 9]$?

why.correct: $[5, 9]$ is exactly one period long, so $f(9) = f(5) = 5$ and the average rate of change is $\frac{5 - 5}{9 - 5} = 0$: the secant line through $(5, 5)$ and $(9, 5)$ is horizontal.
options: The output ends where it started, so the change in output is $0$.
This uses $f(7) = -1$ as an endpoint, $\frac{-1 - 5}{9 - 5}$. The interval ends at $x = 9$, where $f(9) = 5$.
This is $f(9)$ divided by the length of the interval. A rate needs the change in output, $f(9) - f(5)$.
That is the slope of the falling piece on $(5, 7)$, not the slope of the secant line from $x = 5$ to $x = 9$.

items.q: The pattern continues for all $x$. On which interval is $f$ decreasing?

why.correct: In the first cycle $f$ decreases on $(1, 3)$. Adding ten periods ($40$) gives $(41, 43)$.
options: This is $(3, 5)$ plus $40$, where $f$ rises from $-1$ to $5$.
This is $(0, 2)$ plus $40$: $f$ rises on $(40, 41)$ before it starts to fall.
This is $(2, 4)$ plus $40$: $f$ falls only until $x = 43$ and then rises.

items.q: Use the table. What is the building's power use at $t = 52$ hours, in kilowatts?

mistakes.why: That is $P(0)$ or $P(48)$. $52 = 2 \cdot 24 + 4$, so subtract two full days and read $P(4)$.
That is $P(12)$. Subtract whole periods of 24 hours: $52 - 48 = 4$, so the answer is $P(4)$.

why.correct: The period is 24 hours and $52 = 2 \cdot 24 + 4$, so $P(52) = P(4) = 26$ kilowatts.

items.q: What is the average rate of change of $P$ on $[4, 12]$?

mistakes.why: That is the change in power, $64 - 26$. Divide by the change in time, $12 - 4 = 8$ hours.
This divides the change in time by the change in power. Put the change in output on top: $\frac{64 - 26}{12 - 4}$.

why.correct: $\frac{P(12) - P(4)}{12 - 4} = \frac{64 - 26}{8} = 4.75$ kilowatts per hour, the slope of the secant line through $(4, 26)$ and $(12, 64)$.

items.q: The average rates of change of $P$ on $[4, 8]$ and $[8, 12]$ are $6.5$ and $3$ kilowatts per hour. What do these rates suggest about $P$ on $[4, 12]$?
options: $P$ is increasing and its graph is concave down
$P$ is increasing and its graph is concave up
$P$ is decreasing and its graph is concave down
$P$ is increasing at a constant rate of change

why.correct: Both rates are positive, so $P$ is increasing. Over equal 4-hour intervals the rate drops from $6.5$ to $3$, so the rate of change of $P$ is decreasing: concave down.
options: Positive rates: increasing. Smaller rate on the later equal interval: concave down.
Concave up needs the rates to grow over equal intervals; here they shrink from $6.5$ to $3$.
The rates are positive, so the power use is rising, not falling.
A constant rate would give equal rates on the two intervals, but $6.5 \ne 3$.

items.q: What is the average rate of change of $P$ on $[16, 40]$?
options: $0$ kilowatts per hour
$-0.75$ kilowatts per hour
More data beyond $t = 24$ is needed
$\frac{58}{24}$ kilowatts per hour

why.correct: $40 = 16 + 24$, one full period later, so $P(40) = P(16) = 58$. The average rate of change is $\frac{58 - 58}{24} = 0$.
options: The interval is one period long, so the output returns to $58$.
This uses $P(20) = 40$ in place of $P(40)$. Shift by a whole period: $P(40) = P(16)$.
No extra data is needed: the pattern repeats, so $P(40) = P(16) = 58$.
This divides one output by the time. A rate needs the change in output, which is $0$.

items.q: A function $g$ satisfies $g(x + 10) = g(x)$ and $g(x + 5) = g(x)$ for every $x$, and no smaller positive number works. What is the period of $g$?

why.correct: The period is the smallest positive $P$ with $g(x + P) = g(x)$ for all $x$. Both 5 and 10 work, and 5 is smaller.
options: The smallest shift that leaves every output unchanged is 5.
10 works because it is two periods; the period is the smallest shift that works.
15 also works (three periods), but it is not the smallest.
This multiplies the two shifts; the period is the smallest shift that works, 5.

items.q: The brightness $b(t)$ of a lighthouse light seen from a boat repeats every 12 seconds. At $t = 3$ seconds the brightness is $80$ units. Which statement must be true?

why.correct: $27 = 3 + 2 \cdot 12$, two full periods after $t = 3$, so $b(27) = b(3) = 80$.
options: Adding two periods to $t = 3$ gives $t = 27$, with the same brightness.
$9 = 3 + 6$ is only half a period later; the light could be at any brightness then.
Doubling the input does not double the output; nothing says $b(6)$ is $160$.
$36$ is three periods after $t = 0$, so $b(36) = b(0)$, which need not equal $b(3)$.

items.q: A function $f$ has period $2$, and $f(x) = x^2$ for $0 \le x < 2$. What is $f(-0.5)$?

mistakes.why: That squares $-0.5$, but $f(x) = x^2$ only describes the cycle on $[0, 2)$. Add one period: $f(-0.5) = f(1.5)$.
That is $f(2.5)$ from the formula, but $2.5$ is outside $[0, 2)$. Shift $-0.5$ by one period of $2$ to land at $1.5$.

why.correct: $-0.5$ is not in the known cycle $[0, 2)$. Add one period: $f(-0.5) = f(-0.5 + 2) = f(1.5) = 1.5^2 = 2.25$.

items.q: Which quantities are well modeled by a periodic function of time? Select all that apply.
options: The height above the floor of the tip of a clock's minute hand
The number of hours of daylight in a city, over many years
The total distance a car has traveled since it was built
The balance of a savings account that earns compound interest

why.correct: The minute hand repeats every hour, and daylight hours repeat every year. Total distance and a growing balance never return to earlier values.
options: The tip returns to the same height every 60 minutes.
Daylight follows the seasons, so the pattern repeats every year.
Total distance only grows; it never comes back to an earlier value.
Compound interest makes the balance keep growing, not repeat.

items.q: The graph of a periodic function with period 4 is stretched horizontally by a factor of 2: each point $(x, y)$ moves to $(2x, y)$. Predict each change.

variables.name: The period
variables.why: One cycle that took 4 units of input now takes 8, so the period doubles to 8.

variables.name: The greatest output
variables.why: Only the inputs move; every output, including the greatest one, stays the same.

variables.name: The number of full cycles on $[0, 24]$
variables.why: Longer cycles fit fewer times: 24 holds six cycles of length 4 but only three of length 8.

why.correct: A horizontal stretch lengthens each cycle without changing the outputs.

items.q: A function has period 6, and you know its graph on $[0, 6)$. Put the steps for finding $f(53)$ in order.
options: Divide 53 by the period: $53 = 8 \cdot 6 + 5$
Subtract the whole periods: $53 - 48 = 5$
Note that $f(53) = f(5)$, because shifting by whole periods keeps the output
Read $f(5)$ from the known cycle

why.correct: Count the whole periods, remove them, use $f(x + P) = f(x)$, then read the value from the one cycle you know.

items.q: A periodic function $h$ has period 8. What is the average rate of change of $h$ on $[3, 11]$?
options: It depends on the formula for $h$

why.correct: $11 = 3 + 8$, one period later, so $h(11) = h(3)$ and the average rate of change is $\frac{h(11) - h(3)}{8} = 0$.
options: One period apart, the outputs are equal, so the change in output is $0$.
This divides one output by the length of the interval. A rate needs the change in output.
This is one over the period. It is not a rate of change of $h$.
Whatever the formula, $h(11) = h(3)$ because the inputs are one period apart.

items.q: A periodic function $f$ has period 10 and is increasing on $(2, 5)$. On which interval must $f$ also be increasing?

why.correct: Subtracting one period from both ends of $(2, 5)$ gives $(-8, -5)$, where the graph is an exact copy.
options: $(2 - 10, 5 - 10) = (-8, -5)$: a copy of the increasing piece.
This shifts by 5, half a period. Nothing is known about $f$ there.
This interval is longer than the piece where $f$ is known to increase; $f$ may fall on $(5, 12)$.
This shifts by 18, which is not a whole number of periods. A shift of 20 gives $(22, 25)$.
